newsitem.title: USA: Plaintiffs plan appeal in breast implant ruling.
newsitem.headline: Plaintiffs plan appeal in breast implant ruling.

text.p: Lawyers for women suing silicone-gel breast implant makers said on Wednesday they will appeal a federal judge's ruling that there is insufficient scientific evidence to prove the implants cause disease.
The preliminary decision by U.S. District Judge Robert Jones, released on Tuesday, marks the first time a judge has ruled on the hotly debated question of whether or not the implants make women sick.
More than 400,000 U.S. women have filed claims that the implants have caused a variety of health problems, including autoimmune disorders such as lupus and rheumatoid arthritis.
But manufacturers have steadfastly argued there is no scientific link between implants and disease.

Jones' decision bars women in about 70 Oregon cases from using expert testimony to back up claims that implants caused diseases. However, they can still pursue claims that the implants, made by Baxter International Inc, Bristol-Myers Squibb Co and Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing Co, caused localized injuries such as pain and disfigurement from leakage.

The ruling is not binding on cases in other parts of the country and does not affect women with claims against Dow Corning Corp, the nation's largest former breast implant maker, which is trying to reorganize under Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection.

On Thursday, implant plaintiff attorneys were finalizing an alternate reorganization plan for Dow Corning that could result in creditors -- including women with claims -- owning substantial equity in the company.
The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that the plan would initially provide $1.75 billion to creditors.
The proposal also calls for about 30 trials around the country to determine if implants caused diseases in specific women and to help value the claims.
Depending on the outcomes, as much as 95 percent of Dow Corning's common stock could be placed in a trust that would administer payments to creditors, the Journal reported.
Midland, Mich.-based Dow Corning's common stock for more than 50 years has been owned equally by Dow Chemical Co and Corning Inc.
Dow Corning has proposed a single "science trial" with testimony only from medical experts, to settle the question of whether or not implants cause diseases.
About $600 million of the $3 billion plan has been earmarked for out-of-court settlements with women.

Cincinnati attorney Stanley Chesley said the plaintiff's plan of reorganization would result in equity ownership for creditors and said it would firmly reject plans for a single "causation" trial that could prove disastrous for plaintiffs.
"We're not going to play Russian roulette," he said.

In the Oregon case, Jones based his decision on the findings of a four-member "science panel" and 16 studies that he found could not support expert testimony that silicone "more likely than not" causes disease or signs and symptoms of diseases.
However, he said the ruling would not become effective until a medical panel convened by another federal judge in Alabama completes its findings.

"This is a precedent-setting victory," Bristol-Myers Squibb Senior Vice President and General Counsel John McGoldrick said in a statement. "Interested parties all across America have been watching the proceedings in Oregon and this is a major blow to breast implant junk science."

Portland attorney Linda Eyerman, who represents several women affected by the ruling, said it will be immediately appealed. She said Jones' ruling went too far and violated legal precedents that required him to only rule if the metholodology behind the scientific evidence was sound.
"The fact that different scientists may draw different conclusion from the evidence is the reason we have trials," she said.
